planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or small divisions in spring into moist, acidic, gritty, sharply drained soil in a cold, exposed site with reliable winter snow cover.

directions: Blue Heath forms a low mat of tiny needle-like evergreen leaves topped in late spring by nodding, urn-shaped, rose-purple flowers on wiry red stems, a circumboreal arctic-alpine species that reaches its disjunct southern limit on the highest exposed ridges of New Hampshire's Presidential Range. It needs the cool, humid, acidic, and constantly moist-yet-fast-draining conditions of a snowmelt-fed alpine fellfield, and it struggles or dies outright in summer heat, drought, or stagnant soil. Because it resents root disturbance and grows at a glacial pace, it is best started from rooted cuttings set directly into a permanent scree bed or alpine trough rather than transplanted repeatedly. Give it full winter snow cover for insulation and cool root temperatures through summer.

planting.note: Insert rooted cuttings in spring into lean, gritty, well-drained soil in a cold, sunny, wind-exposed site; this willow roots readily and establishes faster than most alpine companions.

directions: Bearberry Willow hugs the ground as a dense, woody mat barely a few inches tall, with rounded, glossy leaves and small upright silvery-gray catkins that emerge before leaf-out, forming extensive carpets on rocky alpine ridges and krummholz-zone ledges from the Arctic south to disjunct outposts in the White Mountains. Unlike the slow, finicky ericaceous alpines it often grows beside, it is one of the easiest arctic-alpine shrubs to propagate, rooting readily from spring cuttings and tolerating more handling during establishment. It still demands sharp drainage, full sun, and a cold root zone, declining in hot, humid, or poorly drained lowland conditions. Its prostrate, gnarled habit and tiny proportions make it a popular subject for alpine troughs, rock gardens, and miniature or bonsai-style plantings.
